questions.q: A guide on a Kannauj heritage walk tells visitors, 'Xuanzang reached India when Harsha's reign was still new.' The chapter puts the start of Harsha's rule at Kannauj in 606, Xuanzang's travels in India from 630 to 644, and Harsha's death in 647. Which correction is right?
questions.a: He arrived 24 years into the reign and left 3 years before Harsha died: 630 - 606 = 24 and 647 - 644 = 3. The 14-year figure is the length of his stay, 644 - 630, and 17 is 647 - 630, the time from his arrival to Harsha's death.
o: He arrived 24 years into the reign and left 3 years before Harsha died
He arrived 24 years into the reign and left 14 years before Harsha died
He arrived 14 years into the reign and left 3 years before Harsha died
He arrived 17 years into the reign and left 3 years before Harsha died

questions.q: Riya wants evidence for the claim 'Kannauj was a flourishing city around 640 CE'. Her library has one account by a Chinese pilgrim who wrote on the Gupta era in the 5th century, and another by a Chinese pilgrim who travelled in India from 630 to 644. Which should she cite, and why?
questions.a: The second pilgrim, Xuanzang: the year 640 falls inside his travels, and he described Kannauj as a beautiful and prosperous city. Faxian wrote about the Gupta era in the 5th century, about two centuries earlier, so his account cannot speak for 640.
o: The second pilgrim, because 640 falls inside the years of his travels
The first pilgrim, because his account of the Gupta era covers all later centuries too
Either pilgrim, because both came to visit sacred Buddhist sites
Neither, because a foreign visitor cannot describe an Indian city

questions.q: Tanvi's group has four items: a copper plate carrying Harsha's signature, a coin with a peacock on the back, Bana's Harshacharita and Xuanzang's travelogue. They want the best source for how Kannauj looked to a visitor from outside India. Which should they use?
questions.a: Xuanzang's travelogue, because he was a visitor from China who described Kannauj as a beautiful and prosperous city. The signature and the coin do not describe the city, and Bana was a poet of Harsha's own court, not an outside visitor.
o: Xuanzang's travelogue
The copper plate with his signature
The coin with a peacock on its back
Bana's Harshacharita, a court biography

questions.q: Harsha held the Prayaga assembly every five years. Suppose one was held in 630, the year Xuanzang's travels began. The first assembly after his travels ended in 644 would fall in the year ___.

Read the statements about Harshavardhana.
1. His rule at Kannauj began in 606 CE.
2. Xuanzang described him as a ruler who stayed away from wars and kept only a small army.
3. Inscriptions show him as a devotee of Shiva, while other sources show him deeply attached to Buddhism.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Xuanzang described a just and energetic ruler who maintained a vast army and was often engaged in military campaigns.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Xuanzang calls Harsha just, energetic and often on campaign, yet the chapter says Harsha achieved only mixed success in uniting northern India. One of them must be wrong.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Neither is wrong: an energetic king often on campaign can still meet strong resistance, as Harsha did from Pulakeshin II and from neighbouring kingdoms. Xuanzang describes the king's character and activity; the chapter describes the outcome.
o: Neither: a busy campaigner can still meet strong resistance
Xuanzang: a visiting pilgrim cannot judge how a king rules
The chapter: a vast army always secures complete victory
Both: Harsha mostly avoided wars and ruled in peace

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Xuanzang's travelogue is a major source of information for historians of Harsha's period.
Reason (R): Xuanzang took more than 600 Buddhist manuscripts back to China.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. A holds because he left a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. The 600 manuscripts are a separate fact about his purpose, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each need of a historian in Column A with the evidence in Column B that the chapter offers for it.
Column A: 1. The title Harsha used for himself  2. A seal issued by Harsha's ally from Kamarupa  3. A Chinese visitor's view of Kannauj  4. Glimpses of courtly life from a work of fiction
Column B: a. Xuanzang's travelogue  b. The novel Kadambari  c. A copper plate signed 'by my own hand'  d. A terracotta seal found at Nalanda
questions.a: The copper plate carries Harsha's own signature and title (c); the terracotta seal found at Nalanda was issued by Bhaskaravarman of the Varman dynasty, Harsha's ally (d); Xuanzang's travelogue is the outsider's account of Kannauj (a); the novel Kadambari gives glimpses of courtly life (b). The distractors swap the seal with the copper plate, or the novel with the travelogue.

questions.q: The chapter's timeline records two events involving the Arabs: the first naval attack, repulsed at Thana, and the conquest of Sindh. Harsha ruled from 606 and died in 647. (a) Which of the two events fell within Harsha's reign, and in which year? (b) How many years after Harsha's death did the other event take place?
questions.a: (a) The first Arab naval attack, repulsed at Thana, in 637 (inside 606 to 647). (b) The conquest of Sindh was in 712, and 712 - 647 = 65 years after his death.
s: Part (a): the Thana naval attack in 637, inside his reign
Part (b): 712 - 647 = 65 years

questions.q: True or False: It is certain that Harsha himself wrote the three Sanskrit plays that historians use to learn about the society of his time. Give a reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says he is assumed to be the author of three plays, so authorship is not certain. Even so, historians can use such literature, as it is, to extract details of governance, social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: he is only assumed to be the author; the use of such literature for details of society does not depend on that

questions.q: A student writes, 'Harsha founded Kannauj as a brand-new capital after leaving Sthaneshvara.' (a) Use the chapter to show that the claim is unsupported: give the city's ancient name and say what Sthaneshvara was to his dynasty. (b) Xuanzang called Kannauj beautiful and prosperous. Does that description tell us how old the city was? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Kannauj was anciently known as Kanyakubja, so it was an old city; Sthaneshvara (Thanesar in Haryana) was only the earlier capital of his Pushyabhuti dynasty. (b) No. It describes the city as the pilgrim saw it in Harsha's time, not when it began.
s: Part (a): ancient name Kanyakubja and Sthaneshvara as the dynasty's earlier capital
Part (b): the description is of the city in his time and says nothing about its age

questions.q: A classmate argues, 'Harsha honoured a Buddhist pilgrim, so he must have been a Buddhist ruler.' (a) What do the inscriptions and the other sources say about Harsha's own belief? (b) Why does this make the classmate's inference weak?
questions.a: (a) Inscriptions depict him as a devotee of Shiva, while other sources say he was also deeply attached to Buddhism. (b) He showed respect for all schools of thought and belief, so honouring one Buddhist visitor does not fix his own faith.
s: Part (a): Shiva devotee in inscriptions, deep attachment to Buddhism in other sources
Part (b): respect for all schools of thought, so one honour proves nothing about his own faith

questions.q: Imagine you are a common citizen watching the Prayaga assembly. A neighbour says, 'This is the assembly Harsha held to honour the Chinese pilgrim.' (a) Correct the neighbour: where was the assembly for the pilgrim held, who attended it, and what was the Prayaga assembly? (b) The wealth at Prayaga went to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor. What does this choice suggest about Harsha, and which sources in the chapter agree?
questions.a: (a) The assembly in the pilgrim's honour was at Kannauj, attended by kings and leaders of many religious sects. The Prayaga assembly, at the meeting of the Ganga and Yamuna, was held every five years, when after sacred rites he gave away much wealth. (b) Giving to Buddhists and Brahmins alike suggests respect for all schools of belief; inscriptions show him as a Shiva devotee while other sources show deep attachment to Buddhism.
s: Part (a): Kannauj for the pilgrim; Prayaga is the five-yearly giving after sacred rites
Part (b): respect for all beliefs, supported by the Shiva and Buddhist references

questions.q: Two accounts of Harsha survive: Bana's biography, written by a poet whom Harsha patronised, and the travelogue of Xuanzang, whom Harsha welcomed to his court. Give three reasons why a historian should still check both against other evidence, such as inscriptions, before accepting them.
questions.a: Any three: Bana was patronised by Harsha, so a court biography may favour him; Xuanzang was welcomed and honoured by Harsha, so his hosts may have shaped what he saw; Xuanzang came as a Buddhist pilgrim, so he may stress Buddhist matters; inscriptions and copper plates are independent evidence made in the king's own time and can confirm or correct them. (These are inferences from the chapter's facts, not statements in it.)
s: A reason linked to Bana's position as Harsha's patronised poet
A reason linked to Xuanzang's welcome or his Buddhist purpose
A reason naming independent evidence such as inscriptions as the check

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Harsha signed as maharajadhiraja, the great king of kings, so his empire must have covered the whole subcontinent.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. A title in a signature does not prove the extent of an empire. The chapter says that its precise extent is not known with certainty, that Pulakeshin II held Harsha in check beyond the Narmada, and that he achieved only mixed success in uniting northern India.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since a title does not prove how far the empire reached
Cites that the extent is not known with certainty or that Pulakeshin II stopped him at the Narmada
Cites mixed success or continuing conflicts with neighbours in the north

questions.q: One student says, 'Xuanzang's travelogue must be accepted as it stands, because he saw everything himself.' Another says, 'It should be set aside, because he came only as a Buddhist pilgrim.' Weigh the two views using the chapter and say how a historian should use the travelogue.
questions.a: For the first view: he travelled in India for 14 years (630 to 644) and kept a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion, so it is a major source. For the second: his purpose was to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn doctrines, and Harsha welcomed him with an assembly, so his picture of a just and energetic king and a prosperous Kannauj may be coloured by this. A historian should use it as a major source while checking it against inscriptions, coins and Bana's work. (The weighing is an inference, not a statement of the book.)
s: States a point for the first view: a long, meticulous eyewitness record
States a point for the second view: his Buddhist purpose
Uses a detail such as the welcome at Kannauj or the praise of Harsha
Names another kind of evidence to check against
A conclusion that the source is valuable but used with checks

questions.q: Write three clues for a quiz so that the answer is 'Xuanzang'. One clue must carry a number, and each clue must use a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct clues, e.g. a Chinese pilgrim; he travelled in India between 630 and 644; he carried more than 600 manuscripts on 20 horses; Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj in his honour.
s: Clue 1 is correct and from the chapter
Clue 2 is correct and carries a number
Clue 3 is correct, new, and the clues together point to him alone

questions.q:
The history club of a Pune school drafts a poster. It reads: 'A Chinese traveller came to India in 630 and left in 644. He came to trade silk. Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj for him and gave away riches at Prayaga every year.' The teacher asks the club to check the poster against the chapter.
(a) Find the two statements on the poster that the chapter does not support, and correct them.
(b) A visitor stays exactly in India from 630 to 644, both years included. At most how many five-yearly Prayaga assemblies could fall in these years?
(c) Name the kind of source the traveller's own writing is, and two things it recorded.
(d) The club can print only one headline: 'A Chinese Eye on Harsha's Court' or 'The King Who Gave Away His Wealth'. Choose one and justify it with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) Not to trade silk, but to visit Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers; and the Prayaga assembly was every five years, not every year. (b) At most 3 (for example 630, 635, 640), since a fourth would need 645. (c) A travelogue; it recorded politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the first draws on the travelogue and Kannauj assembly, the second on the five-yearly giving to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor.
s: Part (a): corrects the trade motive and the yearly Prayaga claim
Part (b): at most 3 assemblies, with the working
Part (c): travelogue, with two things it recorded
Part (d): picks a headline and backs it with chapter evidence

questions.q: Your school museum will display a panel called 'How do we know about Harsha?' with room for three exhibits. Choose three different kinds of evidence from the chapter, say what each shows about Harsha, say one thing each cannot show, and explain in what order you would arrange them.
questions.a: Any three distinct kinds, each with what it shows and a limit, with a reason for the order. For example: the copper plate signed 'by my own hand, great king of kings' shows his title but not how far his empire reached (its extent is not known with certainty); the peacock coin shows he issued coins as a king but not how he ruled; Xuanzang's travelogue shows Kannauj as prosperous and Harsha as just and energetic but comes from a visiting pilgrim; the plays and Bana's work show courtly life but are literature. Order, for instance: his own signature first, then the outsider's account, then literature, moving from the king's voice to others' views.
s: Three different kinds of evidence from the chapter
What each shows about Harsha, correctly
One limit for each exhibit
An order of display
A reason for that order

questions.q:
Aarav finds an old Sanskrit story in the library. It follows a prince and a heavenly woman who meet again across several lives, with one tale placed inside another and brief views of palace life. Its writer died while working on it, and a family member finished it. The writer also served a king at his court and wrote about him in a separate work.
(a) Name the story, its writer and the person who finished it.
(b) Name the writer's separate work about the king, and say which of the two works a historian would use for events of the king's reign, and why.
(c) Say what a historian can still draw from the story, though it is a tale, and what it cannot settle.
(d) For a project on 'Harsha's court as the court saw itself' against 'Harsha's court as a visitor saw it', which of this writer's work or Xuanzang's travelogue would you take as your main source for each? Justify your pairing.
questions.a: (a) Kadambari by Banabhatta (Bana); his son completed it. (b) Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha; for events a historian would turn to the biography, since the story is a romance. (c) Details of courtly life, governance, social diversity and the like, which historians extract from such literature; it cannot settle events or the extent of the king's rule, which need inscriptions and other evidence. (d) Bana's writing for the court's own view, since he was Harsha's patronised poet; Xuanzang's travelogue for the visitor's view, as an eyewitness outsider. Either assignment is acceptable if reasoned, with the limit of each noted.
s: Part (a): Kadambari, Bana, completed by his son
Part (b): Harshacharita, and the biography as the source for events
Part (c): details of society and courtly life usable; events and extent not settled by a tale
Part (d): pairs the court's view with Bana and the visitor's with Xuanzang, with reasons

questions.q: Each of Vikramashila's colleges had its own scholar gatekeeper. If every gatekeeper tests 15 applicants in a day, the university's gates test ___ applicants in a day.

A Class 7 student writes, 'The Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj lasted through the 8th and 9th centuries because each of the three powers had about the same strength.' Which statement from the chapter's summary of the period supports her explanation best?
questions.a: No single power could keep lasting supremacy, because rival states had comparable military strength, administrative systems and strategic approaches. That is why the wars had fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor.
o: Rivals of comparable strength meant that no power could keep lasting supremacy
One power was far stronger but kept losing its gains to revolts at home
The Palas gave up the contest once Dharmapala began founding monasteries
Harsha's heirs kept all three powers away from Kannauj for two centuries

questions.q: A pupil says, 'Harsha died in 647 and the Palas ruled Bengal from then on.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: Bengal fell into disorder after Harsha's death, and only in 750 did the people choose Gopala, the first Pala king, to restore stability. So about 103 years (750 - 647) passed in confusion before Pala rule began.
o: Bengal was in disorder until 750, when the people chose Gopala to rule
Bengal was ruled by Dharmapala from 647, and Gopala was his successor
Bengal was held by the Rashtrakutas until 750, when Gopala defeated them
Bengal was governed by the Pratiharas until Harsha's heirs chose Gopala

questions.q: Ishan's notes say, 'Dharmapala founded Nalanda, Vikramashila and Somapura.' What should his teacher correct?
questions.a: The chapter says Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, while the Palas, just like Harsha, continued to patronise Nalanda, which already existed. So Nalanda is the item to correct.
o: Nalanda: Palas only continued to patronise it
Somapura: it was really founded by Harsha at Kannauj
Vikramashila: it was actually a Chalukya foundation
Nothing needs correcting: Dharmapala founded all three

questions.q: Rahul's notes on the Pala Empire's economy say: (i) internal trade helped the empire flourish; (ii) the east coast seaports gave pathways to Southeast Asia through brisk maritime trade; (iii) the fertile Kaveri delta and efficient irrigation ensured steady agricultural output. His teacher marks one point as an error. Which?
questions.a: The Kaveri delta point: the chapter gives the delta and its irrigation as the prosperity of the Cholas' heartland, not of the Palas. The internal trade and east coast seaport points are what the chapter says of the Palas.
o: The Kaveri delta point, which belongs to the Cholas' heartland
The internal trade point, which the chapter does not link to the Palas
The seaports point, since Pala ports faced the Arabian Sea
The seaports point, since Southeast Asia was reached only by the Cholas

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Several successors of Dharmapala patronised Buddhist institutions and yet were said to be devotees of Shiva.
Reason (R): In ancient India, except perhaps for monks and nuns, people could feel at ease with various belief systems and practise different modes of worship at the same time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. Because belief systems were fluid, a ruler could support Buddhist monasteries while worshipping Shiva.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Palas and the Tripartite Struggle.
1. The Palas won the Tripartite Struggle decisively and held Kannauj for ever.
2. Dharmapala was a great patron of Mahayana Buddhism.
3. The Pala Empire prospered through internal trade and through maritime trade from its east coast seaports.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the struggle was long and indecisive, with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only

questions.q:
Match each number or date in Column A with what it measures in Column B, as the chapter gives it.
Column A: 1. 750 CE  2. The late 8th century  3. Nearly 3,000  4. More than four centuries
Column B: a. how long Vikramashila remained a great centre of learning  b. the year the people chose the first Pala king  c. when Dharmapala founded Vikramashila  d. the number of scholars who studied at Vikramashila
questions.a: 750 CE is the year Gopala was chosen (b); the late 8th century is when Dharmapala founded Vikramashila (c); nearly 3,000 is the number of scholars (d); more than four centuries is how long it stayed a great centre (a). The distractors swap the founding with the election, or the number of scholars with the span of years.

questions.q: Kavya's friend says, 'Three great powers would never fight for an ordinary town.' Using what the chapter tells us about Harsha's reign, give two reasons why Kannauj was worth fighting for.
questions.a: Harsha ruled from Kannauj from 606 CE, so it was the seat of a powerful king who hosted poets and scholars. Xuanzang described it as a beautiful and prosperous city, and Harsha held an assembly there attended by kings and leaders of many sects.
s: One reason: seat of Harsha's powerful kingdom or a city of scholars
Second reason: beautiful and prosperous city, or the great assembly held there

questions.q: True or False: Vikramashila's reach extended beyond India in both directions: it drew students from beyond India, and one of its teachers carried Sanskrit learning to Tibet. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the large monasteries attracted students sometimes from far away, even beyond India, and that a famous teacher of Vikramashila travelled to Tibet, translated Sanskrit works into Tibetan and shaped Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: students came from beyond India, and a teacher took Sanskrit works to Tibet

questions.q: True or False: Vikramashila was destroyed by the Rashtrakutas during the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The struggle among the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas took place in the 8th and 9th centuries, while Vikramashila, founded in the late 8th century, remained a great centre for more than four centuries and was plundered and destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji in the 12th century.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Bakhtiyar Khilji destroyed it in the 12th century, long after the 8th and 9th century struggle

questions.q: Vikramashila was founded in the late 8th century and remained a great centre of learning for more than four centuries. (a) Could it have been destroyed in the 11th century? Use the dates to decide. (b) Who destroyed it, and was he one of the three powers of the Tripartite Struggle?
questions.a: (a) No. Late 8th century (about 780 to 799) plus more than 400 years reaches about 1180 or later, which is the 12th century, not the 11th. (b) Bakhtiyar Khilji plundered and destroyed it in the 12th century; he was not one of the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas or Rashtrakutas.
s: Part (a): no, since adding more than 400 years to the late 8th century passes the 11th
Part (b): Bakhtiyar Khilji, not one of the three powers

questions.q: A student writes, 'Since the Palas alone paid for the big monasteries, learning in India depended on one dynasty.' Give two points from the chapter that go against this view.
questions.a: Harsha too patronised Nalanda, and the Palas only continued that patronage; and the chapter says there were hundreds, if not thousands, of important centres of learning spread across India. So learning did not rest on the Palas alone.
s: First point: Nalanda was patronised by Harsha, and the Palas continued it
Second point: hundreds, if not thousands, of centres of learning across India

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Palas and the Rashtrakutas were already fighting each other for Kannauj in 640 CE.' Show with numbers and dates from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Pala dynasty began when Gopala was chosen in 750, which is 750 - 640 = 110 years after 640. Also Harsha was still ruling from Kannauj in 640 (he died in 647), and the Tripartite Struggle began only after his death, in the 8th and 9th centuries.
s: States that Harsha was alive in 640 and died in 647, and the struggle came after
Calculates 750 - 640 = 110 years before the first Pala king
Concludes that the Palas could not have fought for Kannauj in 640

questions.q: Meena says, 'The Pala kings patronised Buddhist institutions, but that does not mean every Pala king followed only Buddhism.' Is she right? Argue from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Dharmapala patronised Mahayana Buddhism and its monasteries, but the chapter notes that belief systems were fluid, that Harsha and the Guptas patronised several schools, and that several of Dharmapala's successors, while still patronising Buddhist institutions, were said to be devotees of Shiva.
s: Verdict: agrees, patronage did not mean following only Buddhism
Belief systems were fluid in ancient India
Successors patronised Buddhist institutions yet were Shiva devotees

questions.q: Harsha, and some successors of Dharmapala, supported more than one tradition of belief. State the pattern, give the facts for Harsha and for the Palas that fit it, and give the chapter's reason why it was possible.
questions.a: Pattern: rulers patronised several schools of thought. Harsha was shown as a Shiva devotee in inscriptions and as attached to Buddhism in other sources, while respecting all schools; Dharmapala's successors, though patronising Buddhist institutions, were said to be devotees of Shiva. Reason: in ancient India religion was more fluid; apart from monks and nuns, people felt at ease with various belief systems and modes of worship.
s: States the pattern: patronage of several traditions
Facts for both Harsha and the Pala successors
Reason: fluid concept of religion in ancient India

questions.q:
For a role-play on Vikramashila, a Patna school sets up one gate for each college of the university. Forty-eight Class 7 students act as applicants and are shared equally among the gates; a separate student stands at each gate as the gatekeeper. The teacher wants the numbers to match the chapter.
(a) Name the official the gatekeeper students are acting, and say what he did.
(b) According to the chapter, how many colleges did the university have, and so how many applicants stand at each gate?
(c) The chapter gives a figure for the scholars of the whole university. Using it, find the average number of scholars per college.
(d) The principal says a hard gate test will keep the numbers small, while an easy entry will let in students from far away who cannot take a long test. Which should the school's role-play follow? Decide, using what the chapter says about admission and about who came to study.
questions.a: (a) A dvarapandita, the scholar gatekeeper of a college, who tested students before allowing them in. (b) Six colleges, so 48 / 6 = 8 applicants at each gate (the gatekeepers are extra students). (c) Nearly 3,000 scholars / 6 = about 500 scholars per college. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: a hard test matches the highly selective admission of the real university; easy entry matches the way it attracted numerous students from far away, even beyond India.
s: Part (a): dvarapandita who tested students at the gate
Part (b): six colleges, so 48 divided by 6 gives 8
Part (c): nearly 3,000 scholars divided by 6 gives about 500
Part (d): decision justified with selective admission or students coming from afar

questions.q: One student says, 'The Tripartite Struggle was only a waste: it wore the rivals down and left nothing.' Another says, 'The Palas show it was not a waste, since learning and trade grew in the same years.' Weigh the two views using what the chapter says about the struggle and about the Palas, and give your judgement.
questions.a: For the first view: the three powers warred repeatedly in the 8th and 9th centuries with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor, so the long struggle was indecisive. For the second: the Palas, from 750, had Dharmapala found Vikramashila and Somapura, continued to patronise Nalanda, drew students from far away and prospered by internal and east coast maritime trade. Judgement: the contest brought no lasting victor, yet it did not stop the Pala empire from growing in learning and trade, and the empire left a lasting legacy of governance and learning; so the first view is too strong. Either conclusion is acceptable if it uses both sets of facts.
s: Facts for the first view: repeated wars, no lasting victor
Pala monasteries and patronage in the same period
Pala trade, internal and by sea
Notes the legacy after decline
A reasoned judgement that uses both sides

questions.q:
A Kolkata museum prepares a wall panel that begins: 'In 750 CE, after a period of confusion in the region, a leader was picked by the people to bring calm. The ruler who came after him won lands across the east and north and set up two new centres of learning, while continuing to support an older one.' The museum can afford only one extra display.
(a) Name the first king and the dynasty he began, and name his successor.
(b) Name the two new centres of learning and say in which present-day state or country each lies.
(c) The dynasty's ports on the eastern coast opened a route abroad. Name the region it reached and say what this gave the empire.
(d) The choice is between a model of a monastery gate scene and a display on the eastern ports. Which better explains why the dynasty left a lasting legacy? Decide and justify with one chapter fact, noting one fact that supports the other display.
questions.a: (a) Gopala, who began the Pala dynasty; his successor was Dharmapala. (b) Vikramashila (in Bihar) and Somapura (in Bangladesh). (c) Southeast Asia, through brisk maritime trade, which helped the empire flourish economically. (d) Either display is acceptable if reasoned: the gate scene rests on the monasteries as universities drawing students from afar, and on the legacy of learning; the ports display rests on the trade that made the empire prosperous. A fact from the other side must be noted.
s: Part (a): Gopala, Pala dynasty, successor Dharmapala
Part (b): Vikramashila in Bihar and Somapura in Bangladesh
Part (c): Southeast Asia, and the economic benefit of maritime trade
Part (d): display chosen, justified, and a fact from the other side noted

questions.a: Bhillamala was the early Gurjara-Pratihara capital (c); Manyakheta was the Rashtrakuta capital in Karnataka (d); Ellora has the Kailashanatha temple (a); Kannauj was the prize of the struggle and was destroyed a century after Bhoja (b). questions.q: True or False: Amoghavarsha I's reign of 64 years shows that his empire was at peace throughout, since he fought no wars. Give the reason or the correction.

questions.q: The Rashtrakutas were among the most dominant powers for nearly two centuries, and Amoghavarsha I ruled them for a long time. (a) Roughly what fraction of the dynasty's dominant period was his single reign? (b) What does this fraction suggest about the empire's stability?
questions.a: (a) His reign lasted 64 years, and 64 out of nearly 200 is about one third. (b) A single ruler holding the throne for about a third of the dynasty's dominant period gave the empire continuity and stability, as the chapter says of the length of his reign.

Part (b): one long reign gave continuity and stability

questions.q: (a) A 10th-century Arab historian praised a Rashtrakuta ruler, saying Islam was honoured in his kingdom and mosques were always full. What does the remark tell us about the Rashtrakutas? (b) Why should a historian not build the dynasty's whole religious policy on this one remark?
questions.a: (a) It suggests the Rashtrakutas respected and protected Muslims, in line with their patronage of many faiths. (b) It is a single outsider's account; it should be checked against other evidence, such as their equal patronage of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools.
s: Part (a): the ruler respected and protected Muslims in his kingdom
Part (b): one outside remark needs other evidence before it describes a whole policy

questions.q: The chapter says the Gurjara-Pratiharas 'probably originated from western India' and that their capital 'seems to have shifted' to Ujjayini. (a) Give the two clues the chapter uses for a western origin. (b) Why does it use words like 'probably' and 'seems'?
questions.a: (a) The word 'Gurjara' referred to a region between Gujarat and Rajasthan, and their early capital was Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal) in western Rajasthan. (b) These are inferences about early history rather than facts the sources state outright, so the chapter does not claim certainty.

Part (b): they are inferences, not certainties

questions.q: (a) In the mid-8th century Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas in the Deccan. In which direction from Kannauj did this new dynasty's capital lie, and in which present-day state? (b) Did the Chalukya dynasty then vanish for good? Answer with the chapter's later statement.
questions.a: (a) The Rashtrakuta capital, Manyakheta (modern Malkheda), lay in the Deccan, south of Kannauj, in present-day Karnataka. (b) No. A later revival of the Chalukyas in the west, from the 10th century onward, is known as the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
s: Part (a): Manyakheta in Karnataka, in the Deccan to the south
Part (b): the revival from the 10th century as Western Chalukyas of Kalyani

questions.q: Dev says, 'A dynasty that fought many wars could still find the time and money to create great works.' Is he right? Test this claim using the Rashtrakutas.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'Bhoja'. Write three clues, each using a different fact from the chapter, so that the third clue alone rules out Nagabhata I.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct clues, e.g. a devotee of Vishnu; also known as Mihira and Adi Varaha; his empire stretched from Punjab and Kathiawar to Kannauj in the 9th century. The third clue must be one that only fits Bhoja, such as the 9th-century empire reaching Kannauj.

questions.q: Arrange these four events in order and give the century of each: the Rashtrakuta destruction of Kannauj; Dantidurga's overthrow of the Chalukyas; the Ghaznavids' final elimination of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire; Bhoja's empire reaching Kannauj. questions.a: Order: Dantidurga overthrows the Chalukyas (mid-8th century), Bhoja's empire reaches Kannauj (9th century), the Rashtrakuta destruction of Kannauj (a century after Bhoja, the 10th century), the Ghaznavids' final elimination (early 11th century). questions.a: Monument: Krishna I had the Kailashanatha temple, the largest rock-cut temple in India, carved at Ellora. Rashtrakuta action at Kannauj

A reasoned judgement using both sides

questions.q: True or False: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is a collection of inscriptions copied out in order, which is why historians value it. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. It is an epic poem composed in Sanskrit in the 12th century that narrates the history of Kashmir's dynasties from the beginnings to his own time. Inscriptions were only one of Kalhana's sources, along with eleven earlier works and other writings.
s: Verdict: False

questions.q: The chapter says Didda eliminated rivals, including her own grandsons, 'according to Kalhana'. (a) Why does the chapter add those words? (b) Given Kalhana's own ideal of being free from love or hatred, should a reader accept the account as settled? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The words show that the claim rests on one writer's account, which the chapter reports rather than vouches for. questions.q: Differentiate between inscriptions and the Rajatarangini as sources for the rulers of Kashmir, using what the chapter says about each.

The Rajatarangini is a connected narrative composed in the 12th century by Kalhana, who drew on eleven earlier works and inscriptions and also meant to draw moral lessons.
s: Inscriptions: records of the time such as temple consecrations, grants and praise
Rajatarangini: a later connected narrative that used inscriptions and earlier works

questions.q: Compare Kashmir's politics under Lalitaditya Muktapida with its politics after him, giving two features of each as the chapter and the Rajatarangini present them.
questions.a: Under Lalitaditya of the Karkota dynasty, Kashmir was a new power stirring in the mid-8th century and he is seen as a firm ruler, who is said to have defeated an Arab chief three times. questions.q: Rina says, 'Queen Didda was a ruthless schemer and nothing more.' Test her claim against the chapter.

questions.a: No. The chapter says that despite its mountainous geography Kashmir remained well connected to developments elsewhere. It was a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy and arts, and Abhinavagupta's works influenced all of India. s: Verdict: disagrees, since Kashmir stayed connected despite the mountains
Learning, philosophy and Abhinavagupta's wide influence

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because he wanted to draw moral lessons from the ethical values of rulers.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and give two examples from the chapter that show this purpose at work.

First example from the chapter
Second, different example

questions.q:

questions.q: Build a timeline of Kashmir from the mid-8th century to the 12th century for a class display. questions.a: Entries (any four, correctly dated): mid-8th century, Kashmir a new power under the Karkota dynasty, with Lalitaditya Muktapida seen as a firm ruler; after him internal conflicts and shifts of power; late 10th century, Queen Didda consolidates power by alliances and ruthless elimination of rivals, and founds towns and temples; 12th century, Kalhana composes the Rajatarangini. questions.q: Compare Shankaracharya's advaita vedanta with Kashmir Shaivism and analyse what the two together show about intellectual life in this period.
questions.a: Shankaracharya, the 8th-century teacher of advaita vedanta, taught that brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness and that the world we perceive is maya or illusion; he established four mathas at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. Kashmir Shaivism produced scholars such as Abhinavagupta, whose works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics had a vast influence across India. One spread its teaching through mathas in four corners of India and the other through a school of writers in Kashmir. Together they show that philosophy flourished in different regions, with each connected to the rest of the subcontinent.
s: Shankaracharya's teaching on brahman and maya
His four mathas, correctly named
Kashmir Shaivism and Abhinavagupta's works
A comparison of how each spread its influence
Analysis: philosophy flourished in many regions and stayed connected

questions.q:
A guide on the hill above Srinagar (also called Takht-i-Sulaiman, once Gopadri) tells visitors: 'The great 8th-century teacher of advaita vedanta stood right here, and his four monasteries all stand in this valley.' A stone temple at the top is known by two names. The local council can add only one new board: one on the four monasteries, or one on the scholars of Kashmir Shaivism.

(b) Correct the guide's statement about his four monasteries.

questions.a: (a) Adi Shankaracharya; brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness, and the world as we perceive it is maya, an illusion. (b) His four mathas stood at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri, not in the valley. (c) To say that the visit is a tradition and not a proven fact. questions.q:

questions.a: Pulakeshin I founded the Chalukya dynasty (a); his grandson Pulakeshin II held Harsha in check (b); Mahendravarman I was the poet-king whose son Narasimhavarman I was called Mamalla (c); Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Badami (d). questions.q: A student writes, 'Under the southern dynasties, Sanskrit alone was the language of literature.' (a) Give one counter-example from the Pallavas and one from the Eastern Chalukyas. questions.a: (a) The Pallavas promoted Tamil literature as well as Sanskrit; the Eastern Chalukyas saw Telugu and Kannada literature flourish. (b) Dandin; the Pallavas promoted both Sanskrit and Tamil, so their policy supported a classical and a regional language together.
s: Part (a): Tamil for the Pallavas and Telugu or Kannada for the Eastern Chalukyas

questions.q: True or False: The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani were a revival of the same dynasty that had ruled from Badami, not a new family. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter calls them a later revival of the dynasty in the west, from the 10th century onward, with their new capital at Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan in northern Karnataka), after the Rashtrakutas had replaced the Chalukyas in the Deccan by the mid-8th century.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a revival of the dynasty from the 10th century, with a new capital at Kalyani

questions.q: (a) Match each line of Chalukyas to its capital: the Eastern Chalukyas and the Western Chalukyas. (b) Which of the two lines began first, and which words of the chapter show it?
questions.a: (a) The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh; the Western Chalukyas from Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan in northern Karnataka). (b) The Eastern line began first: it asserted independence as the Badami empire declined, whereas the Western line is a revival 'from the 10th century onward'.
s: Part (a): Vengi for the Eastern line and Kalyani for the Western line
Part (b): the Eastern line first, since it began as Badami declined and the Western is a 10th-century revival

questions.q: A guide says, 'The Shore Temple was built in the reign of Narasimhavarman I, who captured Badami.' (a) Using the chapter's caption, correct the king, and say whether the temple therefore belongs to the dynasty's peak under Narasimhavarman I. (b) Mamallapuram also has 'monolithic' temples. What does the word mean?
questions.a: (a) The caption says it was built during the reign of Narasimhavarman II, a later king of the dynasty than Narasimhavarman I, so it was not built in his peak reign. (b) Monolithic means made of a single stone or rock.
s: Part (a): Narasimhavarman II, a later king, so not the peak reign of Narasimhavarman I
Part (b): made of a single stone or rock

questions.q: (a) Which of the Pallavas and the Eastern Chalukyas does the chapter say promoted Buddhist centres? (b) Xuanzang found 100 Buddhist monasteries at Kanchi, the Pallava capital. What does this show about reading a list of a dynasty's patronage?
questions.a: (a) The Eastern Chalukyas, who promoted several Hindu and Jain sects as well as Buddhist centres. (b) The Pallava list names only Jain, Vaishnavite and Shaivite schools, yet Buddhism flourished at Kanchi, so a list of patronage is not complete evidence of who lived or worshipped in a kingdom.
s: Part (a): the Eastern Chalukyas
Part (b): a list of patronage does not show everything present in the kingdom

questions.q: Aarav says, 'Ravikirti's inscription praises Pulakeshin II too highly, so it is useless as evidence.' Is he completely right, partly right or wrong? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, since some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions, so it cannot be trusted blindly. But it is not useless: the chapter checks it against other sources, such as Xuanzang's remark on Pulakeshin II, and concludes there is no doubt that in the early 7th century most of India was dominated by two great imperial powers, Harsha north of the Vindhyas and Pulakeshin II south of them.
s: Verdict: partly right, since the inscription needs checking but is not useless
Poetical style and exaggerations contradicted by other inscriptions
Notes that the chapter itself relies on cross-checking sources rather than dismissing them

questions.q: A student writes, 'By the mid-8th century the Pallavas had replaced the Chalukyas as rulers of the Deccan.' Show from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says that by the mid-8th century it was the Rashtrakutas who replaced the Chalukyas in the Deccan. The Pallavas, after capturing Badami, retreated to keep the Tungabhadra as a boundary, and they themselves were overthrown in the late 9th century by the Chola king Aditya I.
s: States that the Rashtrakutas replaced the Chalukyas
Notes that the Pallavas retreated from Badami to the Tungabhadra boundary, not ruling the Deccan
Pallavas were themselves overthrown by Aditya I in the late 9th century

questions.q: Show with one fact each from the Chalukyas and the Pallavas that these southern dynasties lived with several religious traditions, and say which general statement of the chapter's summary the facts support.
questions.a: Chalukyas: Aihole has over a hundred Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples, and Badami has Hindu and Jain cave temples. Pallavas: they were patrons of Jain, Vaishnavite and Shaivite schools, and Xuanzang noted Buddhist monasteries, Hindu temples and Jains at Kanchi. The summary says that, whatever their own inclination, rulers generally patronised Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, promoting a vibrant cultural pluralism.
s: A fact from the Chalukyas
A fact from the Pallavas
The summary statement about patronage of several traditions

questions.q:
A school heritage trail in Karnataka has three hours at Aihole. The trail leader has read that the site was once the earlier capital of a dynasty that later ruled from a place with famous cave temples, and that a long inscription stands on a hill temple there. The leader must plan the visit.
(a) Name the dynasty and give the old name of Aihole.
(b) The temples at Aihole belong to three traditions. Name them, and say what that mix suggests about the attitude of the rulers, using the chapter's summary.
(c) At the Meguti temple the group will read a long inscription. Name its poet and the king it praises, and say why the guide warns that it must be cross-checked.
(d) With only three hours, should the group spend the longest time on the inscription or on walking through as many temples as possible? Decide, using what the chapter says each can teach.
questions.a: (a) The Chalukyas; Aryapura (later Ayyavole). (b) Hindu, Buddhist and Jain; rulers generally patronised all three, promoting a vibrant cultural pluralism. (c) Ravikirti, the court poet, praising Pulakeshin II; the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, and some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the inscription teaches about Pulakeshin II's victories and how a historian tests a source; the temples show the three traditions side by side at one site.
s: Part (a): Chalukyas and Aryapura
Part (b): Hindu, Buddhist and Jain, and the pluralism of the rulers
Part (c): Ravikirti, Pulakeshin II, and the exaggeration contradicted elsewhere
Part (d): decision tied to what the inscription or the temples teach

questions.q: Your school will take Class 7 to two of these four places for a study tour of the Chalukya-Pallava world: Aihole, Badami, Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram. Choose two, say what the chapter lets students learn at each, name one written source (an inscription or Xuanzang's account) to read at each, and explain why your pair complements each other.

For example Aihole: over a hundred Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples and the Meguti inscription of Ravikirti, which praises Pulakeshin II but needs cross-checking; Kanchipuram: a cultural and trading centre with spices, silk and ivory, and Xuanzang's account of its monasteries, temples and Jains. The pair complements by showing two rival dynasties, the Chalukyas and the Pallavas, with different kinds of source. Mamallapuram offers rock-cut caves, monolithic temples and a seaport with foreign coins; Badami offers its Hindu and Jain cave temples.

What each place lets students learn, correct to the chapter

questions.q: Two sources speak of Pulakeshin II: a long inscription by the court poet Ravikirti, and the remarks of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang. Decide which you would trust more for the claim that he was a powerful king, explain what you would still check, and say what a historian gains by using both together.
questions.a: The inscription, in a highly poetical style, records his victories over Harsha and rival kings, but it is not free from exaggeration and some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions; it was written by his court poet. Xuanzang, an outsider, wrote that his beneficent actions were felt over a great distance and his subjects obeyed him with perfect submission. Since both praise him and neither is free of doubt, a reasoned preference is acceptable, such as the visitor for being outside the court. Still to check: other inscriptions, including those that contradict Ravikirti. Using both together, as the chapter notes of the two imperial powers, supports the firm conclusion that in the early 7th century he was a great power south of the Vindhyas.

Xuanzang's remark on the king

What would still be checked
What the two together support

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Pandya, Chola and Chera kingdoms were already mentioned in an edict of Ashoka as his southern neighbours.

Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.a: Both are true: the chapter says the three kingdoms were named in an edict of Ashoka nearly a millennium earlier, and that they re-emerged in this period. The re-emergence happened centuries later and does not explain why Ashoka named them.

questions.q: (a) Name the two kinds of early evidence the chapter gives to show that the Pandya, Chola and Chera kingdoms existed nearly a millennium before this period. (b) The chapter says they then seemed to disappear. Why should a historian be careful about saying the kingdoms ceased to exist?
questions.a: (a) An edict of Ashoka, which named them as his southern neighbours, and the Sangam literature, the earliest collections of Tamil poetry. (b) They 'seemed' to disappear because other powers eclipsed them in the sources, and they re-emerged later, so silence in the record does not prove they ceased to exist.
s: Part (a): Ashoka's edict and the Sangam literature
