questions.q: True or False: The Pandyas re-emerged at about the time Chola dominance in south India came to an end. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The Cholas swept the Pandyas aside in the 10th century and they re-emerged some three centuries later, which is the 13th century; Chola dominance lasted until the 13th century.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: 10th century plus about three centuries is the 13th century, the century in which Chola dominance ended

questions.q: True or False: The Pandya translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil survives, and historians use it to study the kingdom. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says a copper plate mentions their translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil, but the translation has unfortunately not survived, so historians know of it only from the copper plate.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it is known only from a copper plate; the translation itself has not survived

questions.q: (a) Give the two Chola moves against neighbours that the chapter mentions, with the century of each. (b) Taking Pallava lands to lie in northern Tamil Nadu and Pandya lands in southern Tamil Nadu, did Chola power move north or south between the first move and the second? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Aditya I defeated the Pallavas in the late 9th century, and the Cholas swept the Pandyas aside in the 10th century. (b) South: the first move took northern Tamil Nadu and part of southern Andhra Pradesh from the Pallavas, and the second took southern Tamil Nadu from the Pandyas.
s: Part (a): the Pallavas in the late 9th century and the Pandyas in the 10th
Part (b): south, since Pallava lands lay north and Pandya lands south

questions.q: Explain how two languages were used in a land grant inscription of this period, and suggest one reason for using two.
questions.a: The ruler and his dynasty were praised in Sanskrit, while the operative details of the grant were recorded in the local language. A reasoned suggestion, e.g. Sanskrit gave the grant prestige while the local language let the people concerned understand it.
s: Sanskrit for praise, local language for operative details
A reasonable explanation for using both

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because the fertile delta and efficient irrigation ensured a steady agricultural output.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and name two other things for which the dynasty was known.
questions.a: Question: Why did the Chola heartland remain prosperous? Other things: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy and grand temples (any two).
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First other feature of the Chola empire
Second, different feature

questions.q: Imran says, 'The Pandyas, Cholas and Cheras were often at war with each other, so the Cheras must have been absorbed by their stronger neighbours.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter does say the southern kingdoms were often at war with each other, but it states that the Cheras, also known as Chera Perumals, maintained their independence along the Kerala coast despite their neighbours' military power. The chapter says little more about them, but it gives no sign of absorption.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since the Cheras were not absorbed
Accepts the true part: the southern kingdoms were often at war
Cites the Cheras keeping independence on the Kerala coast despite neighbours' power

questions.q: The chapter lists four things about the Cholas: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy, grand temples, and a fertile delta with efficient irrigation. Choose the two you think mattered most for holding a large empire together, justify the choice, and say what the chapter does and does not tell us about their importance.
questions.a: A reasoned pair is acceptable, such as administration (to govern a large empire) and the navy (to reach beyond the land), or the delta and irrigation (for steady agricultural output in the heartland). The chapter lists these features as the Cholas' strengths and as the heartland's prosperity, but it does not rank them or say which caused the empire to grow.
s: Two features chosen from the chapter's list
A reason linking each to holding a large empire
Notes that the chapter lists the features without ranking them or stating a cause

questions.q:
A museum in Madurai is planning a timeline wall. A volunteer places two cards: 'Pandyas rise to power (6th century)' and 'The Pandyas are swept aside (10th century)'. The director asks her to finish the story.
(a) Which dynasty swept the Pandyas aside, and from which capital did that dynasty rule?
(b) In which century do the Pandyas re-emerge, and how does that compare with the end of the other dynasty's dominance?
(c) A card should record the Pandyas' translation of an epic into Tamil. Name the epic, say what source records it, and why the translation itself cannot be displayed.
(d) The wall has room for a large panel on only one of the two dynasties. Which should it be? Decide and justify with your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Cholas, from Tanjavur. (b) The 13th century, about three centuries after the 10th; this is the century in which Chola dominance ended. (c) The Mahabharata; a copper plate records the translation, which has not survived. (d) Either choice is acceptable if justified: the Pandyas, who rose, fell and returned, with a lost translation known only from a copper plate; or the Cholas, whose dominance ran until the 13th century and who were known for their administration, navy and temples.
s: Part (a): Cholas and Tanjavur
Part (b): 13th century, the century Chola dominance ended
Part (c): Mahabharata, copper plate, not survived
Part (d): panel chosen and justified with the earlier answers

questions.q: The chapter's introduction says some people call this period 'a time of political rivalry and disorder', while a traveller sees 'a land buzzing with new ideas, art, and culture'. Using what you know of the Pandyas, Cheras and Cholas, judge which description fits the south better.
questions.a: For rivalry: the three kingdoms were often at war with each other; the Cholas overthrew the Pallavas in the late 9th century and swept the Pandyas aside in the 10th. For the 'buzzing' view: the Pandyas patronised poets and built rock-cut temples; the Cholas had an elaborate administration, a powerful navy, grand temples and bronzes, and promoted Tamil and Sanskrit; Pandya trade ran through Korkai. The Cheras kept their independence. A reasoned verdict is acceptable, such as that both are true: rivalry between kingdoms went with rich culture and trade within them.
s: Evidence of rivalry in the south
Evidence of culture and learning
Evidence of trade or administration
Handles the Cheras or the Pandya return
A reasoned verdict

questions.q: Build a dated timeline of the Pandyas and the Cholas from the 6th to the 13th century with at least five entries, and say what it shows about whether the rise and fall of kingdoms in this period was permanent.
questions.a: Entries (any five, correctly dated): by the 6th century the Pandyas rise, allied with the Chalukyas and the Pallavas, with Madurai as capital; the Cholas are reborn under Vijayalaya in the 9th century with Tanjavur as capital; in the late 9th century Aditya I overthrows the Pallavas; in the 10th century the Cholas sweep the Pandyas aside; some three centuries later, in the 13th century, the Pandyas re-emerge; Chola dominance lasts until the 13th century. What it shows: the Pandyas fell and returned, and the Cholas rose and then declined, so rise and fall were not permanent.
s: Five entries correctly dated
Entries in the correct order
Both dynasties covered
The re-emergence of the Pandyas included
A conclusion that rise and fall were not permanent

questions.q:
A Chola-era copper plate records the grant of a village to a temple. Its opening lines praise the king and his family in one language, while the later lines, which list the fields and what each family must pay, are in another language.
(a) Name the two languages.
(b) Name the Chola capital and the king who founded it as his new capital in the 9th century.
(c) Which of the two languages would the grant need for the lines on fields and payments if the villagers were to follow them, and why did the grant still use the other language for the king's praise?
(d) A village panchayat in Tamil Nadu must choose between writing every notice twice, in a formal language and in the local language, which costs more, or writing it once in the formal language only. Using the Chola practice, decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit and Tamil. (b) Tanjavur, made the capital by Vijayalaya. (c) The local language, Tamil, for the operative details; the king and his dynastic history were praised in Sanskrit, in the practice of the time. (d) A reasoned decision: writing twice costs more but, as in the Chola grants, the operative details reach those affected in the local language while the formal language gives the ceremonial praise; writing once saves money but those who cannot read the formal language lose the details.
s: Part (a): Sanskrit and Tamil
Part (b): Tanjavur and Vijayalaya
Part (c): Tamil for operative details; Sanskrit for the king's praise
Part (d): decision weighing cost against readers, with the Chola practice

questions.q: Suppose every district (mandala) holds 10 villages and every province holds 5 districts. A king's directly ruled territory consists of 2 bhuktis. It then contains ___ villages.
A teacher reads out four effects of the expanding land grant system and asks which one the chapter presents as a cost rather than a benefit.
questions.a: That powerful intermediaries who did not till the land often exploited peasants is the cost. Bringing uncultivated land under cultivation, expanding crop diversity and supporting agro-based crafts are the benefits.
o: Holders who never tilled often exploited peasants
Uncultivated land was brought under cultivation
Crop diversity expanded across the regions
Cash crops thrived and supported agro-based crafts

questions.q: A student reads that some texts use the word asprishya for communities regarded as 'impure', and concludes that the different varnas and jatis of this period never worked together. Which fact from the chapter corrects her?
questions.a: The chapter says that despite such divisions, different varnas and jatis often functioned cooperatively, because they depended on each other's work and function, at least at the economic level.
o: They often cooperated, since they depended on each other's work economically
Asprishya was a word for foreign traders, who were kept outside the system
Discrimination was a later development that began after the 10th century
Only Brahmanas and Kshatriyas took part in economic life at all

questions.q: Which chain of cause and effect for the period matches the chapter?
questions.a: Better irrigation and agricultural growth let cash crops thrive, and cash crops supported agro-based crafts and industries.
o: Better irrigation and farming growth, then cash crops, then crafts
Cash crops first, then irrigation tanks, then land grants
Land grants first, then urban decline, then irrigation works
Overseas trade, then village tanks, then self-governing villages

questions.q: A student says, 'Merchant guilds of this period were just groups of traders.' Which fact from the chapter corrects her best?
questions.a: The chapter says guilds comprised traders, artisans and moneylenders, and supported religious and charitable activities. So they were broader than traders alone.
o: They included artisans and moneylenders and backed religious works
They were run by samantas who collected tribute for the king's court
They were assemblies that chose the members of each village sabha
They traded only inside one province and never across regions

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls the varna-jati system of this period flexible rather than rigid.
Reason (R): Several sources indicate that the Palas and the Kakatiyas were originally Shudras but in time came to be regarded as Kshatriyas, which shows that such a move was possible.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: dynasties moving from Shudra to Kshatriya status is one of the chapter's examples of how the system varied and was flexible.

questions.q:
Read the statements about administration and land in this period.
1. Provinces were called mandalas and districts were called bhuktis.
2. The land grant system that began under the Guptas expanded greatly.
3. Many inscriptions record the sponsorship of a well, pond or tank, which raised the donor's social status.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: provinces were bhuktis or rashtras and districts were mandalas.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the term in Column B.
Column A: 1. A professional group that became a distinct jati in the 10th century  2. A community that, the chapter says, could remain outsiders  3. A dynasty said to have been originally Shudra and later regarded as Kshatriya  4. A word in a few texts for communities regarded as 'impure'
Column B: a. Foreign traders  b. The Palas and the Kakatiyas  c. The Kayasthas  d. Asprishya
questions.a: The Kayasthas, once scribes, became a jati in the 10th century (c); foreign traders are an example of communities that remained outsiders (a); the Palas and the Kakatiyas were originally Shudras and later regarded as Kshatriyas (b); asprishya, 'not to be touched', appears in a few texts (d). The distractors swap the Kayasthas with foreign traders, or the dynasties with the term for discrimination.

questions.q: The Pallavas built numerous tanks in Tamil Nadu, many of which still work, and many inscriptions record who sponsored a well, pond or tank. (a) Name one gain of such a tank for the land and one for its donor. (b) Why would a donor want the gift recorded in an inscription?
questions.a: (a) For the land, irrigation that supported better farming and agricultural growth; for the donor, a rise in social status. (b) An inscription makes the gift public and lasting, so the donor's raised status is remembered, as the chapter says such sponsorship elevated the donor's social status.
s: Part (a): irrigation for the land and higher status for the donor
Part (b): the record makes the gift public and lasting, keeping the status gained

questions.q: True or False: Samantas were at once indispensable to the kings who ruled through them and a possible threat to those kings. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Samantas led armies and managed local administration, so kings could not do without them; yet their loyalty could be fragile when the central authority seemed to weaken, and some, like the Rashtrakutas, once samantas under the Chalukyas, grew powerful enough to overthrow their overlords.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: they led armies and ran local administration, but loyalty was fragile and some overthrew their overlords

questions.q: Tribhuvana Mahadevi I of the Bhauma-Karas issued grants under the title 'Paramabhattarika Maharajadhiraja Tribhuvana Mahadevi', meaning 'supreme sovereign empress, great queen of the three worlds'. (a) One word in her title also appears in Harsha's signature on his copper plate. Which word, and what does the sharing suggest about her rank? (b) In which century did she rule, and where?
questions.a: (a) 'Maharajadhiraja' (great king of kings); the sharing suggests she claimed the same supreme rank as a king in her own right. (b) The 9th century, in present-day Odisha.
s: Part (a): maharajadhiraja, and the same supreme rank as a king
Part (b): the 9th century in present-day Odisha

questions.q: Compare what Bana's Harshacharita and the inscriptions tell us about women in this period. Give one point from each, and say why the chapter warns against a single description of their position.
questions.a: Harshacharita shows women in agriculture and crafts, and at court as entertainers, musicians, storytellers and attendants. Inscriptions record women making offerings to temples or having water structures built. The chapter says the position of women varied widely between regions and social layers, so one description will not fit.
s: One point from Harshacharita and one from the inscriptions
The position of women varied by region and social layer

questions.q: (a) Name two pieces of evidence from the chapter that show south India's contacts with traders from other lands. (b) Which of the two names the religions of the foreign traders?
questions.a: (a) Any two: a set of copper-plate inscriptions mentioning Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders from West Asia; ancient Chinese, Persian and Roman coins found at Mamallapuram; Pandya coins and inscriptions attesting trade with Southeast Asia via Korkai. (b) The copper-plate inscriptions, which mention Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders.
s: Part (a): two valid pieces of evidence
Part (b): the copper-plate inscriptions name the religions

questions.q: The surname Datta is found among Brahmana families and also among Kayasthas in parts of Bengal. Explain what the chapter says this shows about how the Kayastha jati formed, and give one reason why it makes a rigid reading of varna and jati hard to defend.
questions.a: The Kayasthas began as scribes and clerks, a professional group open to different varnas; certain Brahmana surnames such as Datta later came to be associated with them, which shows a fusion of Brahmana and non-Brahmana families. Over time they married mainly within their group and became a distinct jati in the 10th century. Because a jati could form from a mixed occupational group, the system was flexible rather than rigid.
s: A professional group open to different varnas
Fusion of Brahmana and non-Brahmana families shown by the surnames
Formation of a jati and the link to flexibility

questions.q: A column in a school magazine claims: 'When the big empires fell, the cities of India declined everywhere.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says some historians suggested urban decline but the evidence is more complex. In north India most older cities stayed occupied and new ones emerged; Xuanzang noted the decline of Kaushambi and Shravasti but described thriving Sthaneshvara, Kanyakubja and Kashi. In south India cities flourished, with temples as centres of commerce and ports fuelling maritime trade. 'Everywhere' is wrong.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'everywhere'
North India: older cities occupied, new ones emerged, with Xuanzang's examples
South India: temples and ports sustained cities

questions.q: A textbook note says, 'The varna-jati system of this period was fixed and rigid.' Using three facts from the chapter, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says varna and jati were flexible. The Palas and the Kakatiyas, originally Shudras, came to be regarded as Kshatriyas. New jatis multiplied, based on occupation or region, and tribes and foreign migrants were absorbed into the system. Several bhakti saints were Shudras, and different varnas cooperated economically.
s: States that the chapter calls the system flexible
Palas and Kakatiyas rising from Shudra to Kshatriya status
Another valid fact, e.g. absorption of tribes or the multiplication of jatis

questions.q: Imagine the king's council is debating whether to make large land grants to chiefs and temples. Argue for or against, using the chapter's evidence: give at least two benefits, the main risk, and one step you would take to limit that risk.
questions.a: Either side, if reasoned. Benefits: the grants brought uncultivated land under cultivation, expanding agriculture and crop diversity; irrigation works and agricultural growth supported cash crops and agro-based crafts; grants to religious establishments supported temples. Risk: many holders did not till the land, and powerful intermediaries often exploited peasants. A step to limit the risk, as an inference, could be to attach duties on the holder for the upkeep of tanks, or to keep the peasants' rights written in the grant. Conclusion: stated with a view on whether benefits outweigh the risk.
s: A clear position for or against
First benefit from the chapter
Second benefit from the chapter
The risk stated correctly
A step to limit the risk, with a reason

questions.q:
A guild of ship-owning merchants runs 30 ships: 12 on its west-coast route and 18 on its east-coast route. Its members include traders, artisans and moneylenders. It can afford one new ship this year.
(a) From which century did the west coast see brisk shipping with ports in present-day Iran, Iraq and Africa's east coast?
(b) A set of copper-plate inscriptions mentions Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders from West Asia. Which of the guild's two routes would such traders more likely use, and what do the inscriptions show about India?
(c) The chapter says guilds supported religious and charitable activities, and that temples acted as centres of commerce in south Indian cities. Explain how gifts to a temple could also help a guild.
(d) Should the new ship go to the west or the east route? Decide, using the 12 and 18 ships and what the chapter says each coast connected.
questions.a: (a) The 8th century. (b) The west-coast route, which linked India with Iran, Iraq and Africa's east coast; the inscriptions show India as a hub of international trade. (c) Temples were centres of commerce, so gifts could win goodwill and standing among the traders and artisans who gathered there (an inference from the chapter's two facts). (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the west has only 12 ships but a brisk trade with West Asia and Africa, so a ship would help balance the guild; the east has 18 and reaches Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and Chinese ports, so a ship there adds to a larger, busier route.
s: Part (a): 8th century
Part (b): west-coast route, and India as a hub of international trade
Part (c): temples as centres of commerce, so gifts bring standing among traders
Part (d): decision justified with the ship numbers and the chapter

questions.q: Explain how a king of this period ruled his core regions and distant regions, and analyse one advantage and one challenge of this system.
questions.a: Kings like the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas ruled their core regions directly, dividing them into provinces, districts and villages with officials at every level, and governed other regions through samantas. Villages were largely self-governed under headmen, accountants and local committees, and south India saw assemblies at several levels. The advantage was that samantas led armies and ran local administration, so the king need not control every region. The challenge was that their loyalty could be fragile when the centre looked weak, as when the Rashtrakutas overthrew the Chalukyas.
s: Direct rule of the core regions
Rule through samantas elsewhere
Levels of administration and the self-governing village
An advantage of the system
A challenge with the Rashtrakuta example

questions.q:
On a temple wall in a Tamil Nadu village, a long 10th-century inscription lays down how the members of the village council are to be chosen. A Class 7 group compares it with the way their own school council is selected.
(a) Name the dynasty that issued the inscription and the council it describes.
(b) Name two officials or bodies, besides the council, that oversaw a village in this period.
(c) By the 9th century, what kind of bodies had risen in south India, according to the chapter?
(d) A group member says, 'One inscription from one village shows that democratic traditions in all of India ran unbroken for 1,500 years.' Does the chapter support this, and what can the inscription not show? Decide.
questions.a: (a) The Cholas; the village sabha at Uttaramerur. (b) Any two of headmen, accountants and local committees. (c) Assemblies at several levels. (d) The chapter does draw this conclusion: the inscription showed the long continuity of democratic traditions in India, back 1,500 years to the janapadas. But one inscription from one village cannot by itself show how every place was governed or how widely such selection was used; it supports the chapter's claim only together with other evidence such as the assemblies of the 9th century.
s: Part (a): Cholas and the village sabha
Part (b): two valid officials or bodies
Part (c): assemblies at several levels
Part (d): decision noting the chapter's claim and the limit of one inscription

questions.q: A lecture says, 'Mahavira, the author of the first mathematics work independent of astronomy, was the great Jain teacher.' Which pair of details from the chapter shows the lecturer is wrong?
questions.a: The mathematician lived at the court of the 9th-century Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha Nripatunga, while the great Jain teacher of the same name lived over a millennium earlier. The chapter warns that they are not to be confused.
o: Amoghavarsha's 9th-century court, against a teacher a millennium earlier
Harsha's court at Kannauj, against a teacher born in 598 CE
A pupil of Brahmagupta, against a teacher of the 6th century CE
A writer in Persian, against a teacher who wrote in Latin

questions.q: The chapter names 12 Alvars and 63 Nayanars as the first great bhakti poet-devotees of the South. Taking all of them together, the percentage who were devotees of Shiva is ___ per cent.
A student wants to describe the route by which Brahmagupta's rules reached Europe. Which description fits the chapter?
questions.a: His works were translated into Persian and later into Latin, contributing to the growth of mathematics in the Arab world and, later, Europe. So the Arab world came first and Europe later.
o: Persian first, then Latin, helping the Arab world first and Europe later
Latin first, then Persian, helping Europe first and the Arab world later
Greek first, then Arabic, helping Europe alone
Chinese first, then Latin, helping the Arab world alone

questions.q: A 9th-century monastery in eastern India teaches meditation and mantras, and its monks revere powerful deities, especially Shakti. It is supported by a dynasty with great monastic universities. Which pair fits the chapter?
questions.a: Buddhism partly influenced by Tantricism, which emerged around the 6th century and stressed rituals, meditation, mantras and powerful deities, thrived in eastern India under the Palas.
o: Tantric influence on Buddhism, under the Palas
Bhakti of the Alvars, under the Palas
Tantric influence on Buddhism, under the Rashtrakutas
Jainism of the Bahubali tradition, under the Palas

questions.q: A guidebook says, 'Jainism in this period was confined to Karnataka.' Which fact from the chapter corrects this best?
questions.a: The chapter says Jainism remained popular in western India and Karnataka, with the Jain cave temples at Ellora in Maharashtra as well as at Badami in Karnataka. So it was not confined to Karnataka.
o: Jainism was popular in western India too, as Ellora's caves show
It was patronised only by the Palas of Bengal and their courts
It had spread to the South through the Alvars and Nayanars
It was replaced by Tantric schools throughout Karnataka

questions.q: The chapter notes that one of the 12 Alvars was a woman and that three of the 63 Nayanars were women. A student compares the two groups. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Women were 1 of 12 Alvars (about 8.3 per cent) and 3 of 63 Nayanars (about 4.8 per cent), so they were a larger share of the Alvars.
o: A larger share of the Alvars (1 of 12) than of the Nayanars (3 of 63)
A larger share of the Nayanars (3 of 63) than of the Alvars (1 of 12)
An equal share in both groups, about 5 per cent
More than 10 per cent of all the 75 devotees

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhakti poetry reached people across gender and social divisions and reshaped Indian society and literature.
Reason (R): Bhakti poetry, composed mostly in regional languages, invoked a direct personal relationship with the divine that was open to everyone.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because the poetry was in regional languages and offered a personal relationship with the divine open to everyone, it cut across gender and social divisions.

questions.q:
Read the statements about religion in this period.
1. The 12 Alvars were devotees of Shiva and the 63 Nayanars were devotees of Vishnu.
2. The initial spark of the bhakti spread came from the South, in devotional literature written in Tamil.
3. Tantric schools emerged around the 6th century and rejected all rituals in favour of silent devotion.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. Statement 1 swaps the deities: the Alvars were devotees of Vishnu and the Nayanars of Shiva. Statement 3 is false: the Tantric schools emphasised rituals, meditation, mantras and the worship of powerful deities, especially Shakti.

questions.q: (a) The chapter says several bhakti saints belonged to one varna in particular. Name it. (b) Using that fact and the presence of women among the Alvars and Nayanars, explain how bhakti 'cut across' divisions in society.
questions.a: (a) Shudras. (b) Bhakti saints emerged from diverse social backgrounds, including Shudras, and included women, so its devotion open to everyone was not limited by varna or gender.
s: Part (a): Shudras
Part (b): saints of different varnas and women, so devotion open to all across divisions

questions.q: True or False: Bhakti began as an organised movement founded in the 6th century by the Alvars and the Nayanars. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says bhakti, devotion addressed to a deity, existed much earlier; what happened from the 6th century was its massive spread among all layers of society and across India, rather than an organised movement, with the initial spark from the South.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: bhakti existed earlier; from the 6th century it spread widely, not as an organised movement

questions.q: A student says, 'The mathematics of this period was of no use outside the study of the sky.' (a) Name two practical objectives that the chapter says motivated these scholars. (b) Give one example from the chapter of a mathematician's work being used far from where it was written.
questions.a: (a) Preparing reliable calendars and making precise predictions of solar and lunar eclipses. (b) Brahmagupta's works were translated into Persian and later Latin, helping mathematics grow in the Arab world and Europe.
s: Part (a): calendars and eclipse predictions
Part (b): Brahmagupta's works translated into Persian and Latin

questions.q: Differentiate the Tantric schools from the bhakti tradition, giving one defining feature of each as the chapter describes them.
questions.a: The Tantric schools, which emerged around the 6th century, emphasised rituals, meditation, mantras and the worship of powerful deities, especially Shakti. The bhakti tradition emphasised personal devotion to a deity over Vedic sacrifices, open to all and composed mostly in regional languages.
s: Tantric schools: rituals, meditation, mantras, powerful deities such as Shakti
Bhakti: personal devotion open to everyone, often in regional languages

questions.q: The chapter shows a statue of Karaikal Ammaiyar, a woman saint who probably lived in the 6th century CE. (a) To which group of poet-devotees did she belong, and which deity did that group worship? (b) What does her probable century tell us about when women appear in the spread of bhakti?
questions.a: (a) She was one of the Nayanars (Nayanmars), devotees of Shiva. (b) The 6th century is when bhakti began its massive spread, so women were among the poet-devotees from the earliest period of that spread.
s: Part (a): the Nayanars, devotees of Shiva
Part (b): women appear from the 6th century, the start of the spread

questions.q: Two scholars of this period are linked in the chapter to things you learn in Grade 7 mathematics. Name them, say what each is linked to, and say what this shows about the roots of school mathematics.
questions.a: Brahmagupta introduced the rules of arithmetic with zero, negative numbers and fractions, the same ones learnt at school. Virahanka was the first to establish the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence. This shows that parts of school mathematics have roots in the work of Indian scholars of this period.
s: Brahmagupta and the rules for zero, negative numbers and fractions
Virahanka and the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence
The roots of school mathematics in Indian scholarship

questions.q: An answer key says: 'The 63 Nayanars, devotees of Shiva, including three women.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and add two further facts about the tradition that the Nayanars belonged to.
questions.a: Question: Who were the Tamil poet-devotees of Shiva who gave the initial spark to the spread of bhakti? Further facts: they produced devotional literature in Tamil with an enormous impact; the Alvars, 12 devotees of Vishnu, were the other group; bhakti spread from the 6th century across all layers of society.
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First further fact
Second further fact, different from the first

questions.q: Dev says, 'Buddhism declined all over India in this period because kings stopped supporting monasteries.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. In eastern India Buddhism thrived, partly influenced by Tantricism, especially under the Palas, whose monastic universities drew scholars from across Asia. Elsewhere it did decline, and the chapter links this to the rise of temple-based Hinduism and bhakti practices; it does not say that rulers withdrew their support, and it notes that rulers generally patronised several traditions.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'all over India'
East: it thrived under the Palas and their monastic universities
Elsewhere: decline came alongside the rise of temple-based Hinduism and bhakti; the chapter does not say royal support was withdrawn

questions.q: Design a one-page pamphlet titled 'Minds of the Age' for your school library on the mathematicians of this period. Choose three scholars from the chapter, give one contribution of each, state the practical purposes behind such work, and explain why royal patronage mattered.
questions.a: Any three of: Brahmagupta (rules for zero, negative numbers and fractions, solving equations, translated into Persian and Latin); Bhaskara I (pioneering trigonometry, commentary on the Aryabhatiya); Virahanka (the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence); Mahavira (first mathematics work independent of astronomy, at the court of Amoghavarsha). Purposes: reliable calendars and precise predictions of solar and lunar eclipses, as well as pure search for knowledge. Patronage: such a long tradition would not have been possible without royal patronage, as with art and literature.
s: Three scholars chosen from the chapter
A correct contribution for each of the three
Practical purposes: calendars and eclipse predictions
The role of royal patronage
Clear organisation of the pamphlet

questions.q: A student writes, 'Bhakti was a revolution that appeared suddenly in the 6th century and replaced the earlier religious traditions of India.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Bhakti, devotion addressed to a deity, existed much earlier; what happened from the 6th century was its massive spread among all layers of society, rather than an organised movement. The initial spark came from the South, from the 12 Alvars and 63 Nayanars composing in Tamil. Other traditions continued: Jainism remained popular in western India and Karnataka, Buddhism thrived in eastern India under the Palas, and Tantric schools emerged. Buddhism declined elsewhere as temple-based Hinduism and bhakti rose. Verdict: the statement is wrong on 'suddenly' and on 'replaced', though bhakti's spread did reshape society and literature.
s: Bhakti existed earlier
The 6th-century change was a massive spread, not an organised movement
The southern spark by the Alvars and Nayanars
Other traditions that continued or declined
A reasoned verdict

questions.q:
A maths club prepares a poster: 'A mathematician born in 598 CE in a western Indian city that later became a royal capital wrote a book that laid down how to work with zero, negative numbers and fractions, and found ways to solve some equations. His books crossed languages and continents.' The club wants to name its Maths Day after one scholar of this period.
(a) Name the scholar and the city, and the dynasty whose first capital it became.
(b) Name the two languages his books passed through and say what that order shows about how knowledge travelled.
(c) The chapter says one other mathematician wrote something that no other mathematician of the period did. Name him and the work.
(d) Should the day be named after the scholar on the poster or after the one in (c)? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Brahmagupta; Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal), later the first capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. (b) Persian and later Latin; his work passed through the Arab world to Europe, so knowledge moved in stages across regions. (c) Mahavira, who lived at the court of Amoghavarsha Nripatunga and wrote the first work of mathematics independent of astronomy. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: Brahmagupta's rules for zero and negatives are the ones students use and his work travelled widely; Mahavira marks mathematics becoming a subject independent of astronomy.
s: Part (a): Brahmagupta, Bhillamala, Gurjara-Pratiharas
Part (b): Persian then Latin; knowledge moved in stages to the Arab world and Europe
Part (c): Mahavira and the first mathematics work independent of astronomy
Part (d): decision justified from the chapter

questions.q:
A school tour of Karnataka and Maharashtra stops at a tall monolithic statue made in the 10th century. The guide says it shows a revered figure meditating for 12 years until an anthill rose behind him and plants climbed his limbs. The leader can add one more stop, either a Pallava rock-cut site in Tamil Nadu or Ellora in Maharashtra, to support the theme 'rulers supported many faiths'.
(a) Name the statue and the town where it stands.
(b) Where did Jainism remain popular in this period, and who supported it?
(c) Name the Hindu temple and the Jain monuments linked with Ellora or Badami in the chapter, and the dynasty whose patronage covered Ellora.
(d) Which extra stop better supports the theme? Decide, and justify with one chapter fact about the chosen stop and one about the other.
questions.a: (a) Bahubali, at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka. (b) In western India and Karnataka, supported by rulers and wealthy merchant communities. (c) The Hindu Kailashanatha temple and the Jain cave temples at Ellora or Badami; the Rashtrakutas, who equally patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: Ellora puts a Hindu temple and Jain caves in one place under a dynasty that patronised all schools; the Pallava site shows patronage of Jain, Vaishnavite and Shaivite schools through its rock-cut caves.
s: Part (a): Bahubali and Shravanabelagola
Part (b): western India and Karnataka; rulers and merchants
Part (c): Kailashanatha temple, Jain caves, and the Rashtrakutas
Part (d): choice justified with a fact on each stop

questions.q: A museum caption reads, 'The Hunas ruled the Ganga plains until the 7th century, when they were driven out.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The Hunas pushed deep into the Ganga plains in the early 6th century and were defeated by the Aulikara kings of Dashapura, which effectively ended Huna power in India. By the 7th century they had assimilated into Indian society as soldiers and local officials.
o: Their power ended in the early 6th century; by the 7th they had settled in India
Their power ended in the 8th century, when Arab armies crushed them in Sindh
They were never defeated and ruled the Ganga plains until the Pratiharas
They were expelled by Harsha and returned to Central Asia in the 7th century

questions.q: A student compares two sources on the fall of Debal: Al-Baladhuri, a 9th-century Arab historian, and the Chachnama, a 13th-century Persian rendering of an older Arabic account. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Al-Baladhuri wrote about four centuries before the Chachnama's 13th-century rendering (13 - 9 = 4), so he is nearer in time to 712, but neither was an eyewitness of the events of 712.
o: Al-Baladhuri is nearer to 712 by about four centuries, though no eyewitness
The Chachnama is nearer in time to 712, as it renders an older account
Both are eyewitness records, since both describe the fall of Debal
Both are equally distant from 712, as both are Muslim sources

questions.a: 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact compared with conquests elsewhere, and Hindus and Buddhists could rebuild temples and worship.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After about three centuries of effort, Arab dominion in India was limited to just two petty states, in Sindh and Punjab.
Reason (R): Indian rulers never joined hands against the Arabs.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: the geographer al-Istakhri observed this. R is false: the chapter says Indian rulers offered stubborn resistance and sometimes forged alliances to defeat the Arabs.

questions.q:
Match each source in Column A with the claim it supplies in Column B.
Column A: 1. Al-Baladhuri, a 9th-century historian  2. The Chachnama, a 13th-century Persian rendering  3. Sulaiman, a 9th-century Arab merchant  4. Al-Istakhri, a geographer
Column B: a. After three centuries of effort the Arab dominion was limited to two petty states  b. The slaughter of the inhabitants of Debal went on for three days  c. There is no greater foe of the Muhammadan faith than a Pratihara ruler  d. Bin Qasim declared it his bounden duty to carry on a religious war
questions.a: Al-Baladhuri describes the slaughter at Debal (b); the Chachnama records bin Qasim's declaration of a religious war (d); Sulaiman calls the Pratihara ruler the greatest foe of the Muhammadan faith (c); Al-Istakhri observed that after three centuries the dominion was limited to two petty states (a). The distractors swap the two writers on the conquest or the merchant with the geographer.

questions.q: (a) According to the Chachnama, how did Muhammad bin Qasim describe his reason for fighting King Dahar? (b) The Chachnama is a 13th-century Persian rendering of an older Arabic account. Why should a historian handle it with care as evidence for 712?
questions.a: (a) He said it was his bounden duty to carry on a religious war in obedience to the orders of God. (b) It was set down in Persian about five centuries after the events (13th century against 712 in the 8th) and is a rendering of an older account, so it is not an eyewitness record and should be checked against other sources.
s: Part (a): a bounden duty to carry on a religious war in obedience to God's orders
Part (b): written about five centuries later and a rendering of an earlier account, so needs cross-checking

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the Hunas of Indian literature 'are thought to have been' a branch of the Huns. What does the wording tell you about the evidence? (b) Which dynasty's kings defeated two Huna leaders, and from which capital did they rule?
questions.a: (a) The link between the Hunas and the Huns of Central Asia is a reasoned belief, not a certainty. (b) The Aulikara dynasty, whose capital was Dashapura, modern Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh.
s: Part (a): 'thought to' shows the link is likely but not certain
Part (b): Aulikara dynasty, capital Dashapura (Mandsaur)

questions.q: A 7th-century inscription records a Huna serving on the administration council of a temple. A student says this contradicts the picture of the Hunas as fierce conquerors. (a) Explain why it does not, using the chapter's timeline. (b) Name two Gupta-style features that the Hunas adopted and that a historian could check on their coins.
questions.a: (a) The Hunas' invasions were in the early 6th century and ended when the Aulikara kings defeated their leaders; by the 7th century they had assimilated into Indian society, serving as soldiers and in local administrations, so a Huna on a temple council fits. (b) Gupta-style royal titles, coin designs and religious symbols, such as the goddess Lakshmi and attributes of Vishnu or Shiva (any two).
s: Part (a): conquest in the early 6th century, assimilation by the 7th
Part (b): two Gupta-style features such as titles, coin designs or religious symbols

questions.q: Al-Baladhuri says bin Qasim kept up the slaughter at Debal for three days and had a great temple destroyed. The chapter also says that in Sindh Hindus and Buddhists were later allowed to rebuild temples and priests kept their share of revenue. (a) Do the two accounts contradict each other? Explain. (b) Does the chapter say why the policy changed?
questions.a: (a) No. The first describes the conquest of Debal and the second a later change of Arab policy in Sindh; both can be true at different times. (b) It gives two possibilities, strategic reasons or compulsion, and does not decide between them.
s: Part (a): no contradiction; the first is the conquest, the second a later change of policy
Part (b): strategic reasons or compulsion, undecided

questions.q: True or False: The decimal numerals with zero were invented by the Arabs, which is why they are called 'Arabic numerals'. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The system is Indian in origin: Arab mathematicians themselves acknowledged its Indian origin, and the numerals were called 'Arabic' only because the Arabs transmitted them to Europe; several dictionaries now add the term 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Indian origin, acknowledged by Arab mathematicians; 'Arabic' reflects their transmission to Europe

questions.q: The chapter draws on sources from both sides of the Arab-Indian contest. For each of Al-Baladhuri, the Gwalior inscription and the Rajatarangini, say whether it comes from the Arab or the Indian side and give one claim it supplies.
questions.a: Al-Baladhuri is an Arab-side historian, and he reports that bin Qasim kept up the slaughter at Debal for three days. The Gwalior inscription is Indian, and it records that Nagabhata I crushed the large army of the Mlechchha king. The Rajatarangini is Indian, by Kalhana, and it says that Lalitaditya defeated an Arab chief three times.
s: Al-Baladhuri: Arab side, with a correct claim
Gwalior inscription: Indian side, with a correct claim
Rajatarangini: Indian side, with a correct claim

questions.q: Sameer says, 'Every foreign invader who came to India in this period ended up as a part of Indian society.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says foreign invaders often assimilated and owned India's cultural traditions: the Hunas by the 7th century served as soldiers and in local administrations, used Sanskrit and Prakrit and adopted Gupta-style titles and coins. But 'every' is wrong: the chapter adds that with the advent of Islam the situation changed, and the Arabs struggled for a long time and kept only two petty states.
s: Verdict: partly right
The part that holds: the Hunas assimilated, with evidence
The part that fails: with Islam the situation changed, so not every invader assimilated

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because Indian rulers resisted stubbornly and sometimes forged alliances.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and add two facts from the chapter that show this resistance.
questions.a: Question: Why were the Arabs frustrated for a long time in their advances into India? Facts (any two): Indian chiefs rebelled within two years of Qasim's death and regained most of the territory; Nagabhata I crushed a large Arab army; Lalitaditya defeated an Arab chief three times; Arab dominion shrank to two petty states.

First supporting fact
Second supporting fact, different from the first

questions.q: 'The Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact.' Justify this statement from the chapter.
questions.a: Indian chiefs rebelled within two years of Qasim's death and regained most of the conquered territory. Further Arab advances into Rajputana and Malwa were short-lived because rulers like Nagabhata I crushed their armies and Lalitaditya defeated an Arab chief three times. Al-Istakhri observed that after three centuries their dominion was limited to two petty states in Sindh and Punjab, where they survived only by giving up iconoclasm and using native Hindus and Buddhists. In Sindh, Hindus and Buddhists were allowed to rebuild temples and worship, and priests kept their share of revenue. This contrasts with other regions where Islam replaced local institutions and led to mass conversions.
s: Revolt and recovery of territory
Short-lived gains and Indian victories
Al-Istakhri's observation about two petty states
Change in policy: temples and priests' revenue
Contrast with other regions

questions.q: Compare the invasions of the Hunas and the Arabs in their origin, methods, resistance faced and long-term impact on India.
questions.a: The Huns were nomads from Central Asia with horse-riding and archery skills and lightning-fast attacks, and the Hunas of Indian literature are thought to be a branch of them; the Hunas pushed into the Ganga plains in the early 6th century. The Arabs came from the newly expanded Islamic world, first with naval raids in 637 and then with an army into Sindh under Muhammad bin Qasim. The Hunas were defeated by the Aulikara kings, while the Arabs were frustrated for centuries by the stubborn resistance of Indian rulers like Nagabhata I and Lalitaditya, and their dominion shrank to two petty states. The Hunas were assimilated into Indian society, adopting its language, titles and symbols. The Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact, though trade and the exchange of ideas such as the numerals continued.
s: Origin and methods of the Hunas
Origin and methods of the Arabs
Resistance each faced
Outcome for the Hunas: assimilation
Outcome for the Arabs: limited impact and cultural exchange

questions.q:
A 9th-century Arab merchant, Sulaiman, wrote about an Indian ruler: 'He maintains numerous forces, and no other Indian prince has so fine a cavalry. He is unfriendly to the Arabs; there is no greater foe of the Muslim faith than he. There is no country in India safer from robbers.' A Gwalior inscription of the same dynasty says one of its early kings crushed the large army of a 'Mlechchha king'.
(a) Name the dynasty and the early king.
(b) Why would an Arab merchant call the ruler a foe of his faith?
(c) What do the merchant's praise of the cavalry and of the roads suggest about how this dynasty ruled?
(d) One historian says the merchant's words can be trusted fully because he was a witness; another says that Arab-side accounts such as Sulaiman's and Al-Baladhuri's all see events from one side. Decide how far each is right, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Gurjara-Pratiharas; Nagabhata I. (b) The dynasty pushed back Arab invasions into northwest India, so the Arabs saw him as an enemy. (c) A strong, well-organised state with large forces that kept order, which also fits its success in resisting the Arabs. (d) Partly each: Sulaiman saw the kingdom himself and his picture fits the Gwalior inscription, but he writes from the Arab side as a merchant, as do Al-Baladhuri and others, so Indian sources are needed to check the judgement. A reasoned view is accepted.
s: Part (a): Gurjara-Pratiharas and Nagabhata I
Part (b): the dynasty pushed back Arab invasions
Part (c): strong forces and order in the dynasty's rule
Part (d): reasoned judgement about an outsider's evidence

questions.q:
A museum places two coins side by side. One is a coin of the Huna ruler Toramana, with his name 'Tora' in Brahmi script; the other is a coin of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta. They look strikingly similar. A panel adds that an inscription records a Huna serving on the administration council of a temple.
(a) The Hunas are thought to be a branch of which Central Asian people, and the kings of which dynasty ended their power in India?
(b) Name the temple's council, and say what a Huna's seat on it shows about the Hunas by the 7th century.
(c) Which coin shows borrowing, and what else did the Hunas borrow in the same way?
(d) The museum can afford one more exhibit: a model of a Huna cavalry raid of the early 6th century, or a model of a temple council meeting. Choose one and justify it with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) The Huns; the Aulikara kings of Dashapura (Mandsaur). (b) The goshthika; it shows that by the 7th century the Hunas had assimilated into Indian society and held local roles. (c) The Huna coin borrows Gupta-style designs; they also used Gupta-style royal titles and religious symbols and adopted Sanskrit and Prakrit for inscriptions. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the raid rests on their fast attacks that pushed deep into the Ganga plains in the early 6th century despite stiff resistance; the council meeting rests on their assimilation by the 7th century.
s: Part (a): the Huns, and the Aulikara kings who ended their power
Part (b): goshthika, showing assimilation and local roles
Part (c): the Huna coin borrows Gupta designs; also titles, symbols, Sanskrit and Prakrit
Part (d): exhibit chosen and justified with chapter evidence
